title: As Budgets Tighten, More People Are Dusting Off Their Library Cards
summary: When money gets tight, a lot of people reach for the same thing: a library card. Izzy Rivera, who lives in Topeka, Kansas, reads at least one book every week. But as she saves up for law school, buying new books is not always in her budget. "Say I'm buying a few a month," she said, "it just isn't realistic." So Rivera borrows books and digital copies from her local library through the Libby app. Last month she picked up 15 books for about $20 at her library's used book sale. "It's somewhere I can go where I'm not expected to spend money," she said. A Pew Research Center survey released in mid-October found that 44% of Americans say they have struggled in the past year to afford at least one basic necessity, and 70% said they have cut back on extras such as streaming subscriptions. Several of the largest public library systems in the country have reported recent rises in membership, borrowing and event attendance. Librarians say the rising cost of living is part of the reason. In Los Angeles, use of the library's makerspace grew 37%, while digital borrowing and visits were both up more than 20%. There is history behind the trend: library borrowing rose at 18 large systems during a brief U.S. recession in 2001. Libraries have also become places to borrow more than books. Many lend out Wi-Fi hotspots, cooktops, birding kits and camping gear, in what is often called a "library of things." At the same time, library funding is under pressure. Last year, the Trump administration tried to cut the federal Institute of Museum and Library Services, but 21 states sued and the grants were restored. Maria McCauley, president of the American Library Association, said libraries rely on a mix of federal, state and local funding.
why_it_matters: Libraries give everyone free access to books, movies, tools and help, which matters most when money is tight.
